<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-nass-autoplot-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-nass-autoplot" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-nass-autoplot</p>
</div>

The dashed line is the model-averaged prediction over the retained equations, and
the grey band is its 95% credible interval. The band is narrow wherever a dose was
tested, and opens across the interval from 1.25 to
2.5, where none was, because the curve has to fall
somewhere in that interval and the data do not indicate where. The solid line is
the model-averaged *N(S)EC*, and the dotted lines are its bounds, at
0.33 and 1.92, which lie
on either side of the lower end of that untested interval. The axis is the one
used for the raw-data figure, so the control keeps its marked position, and the
nine doses at or below 1.25 are legible instead of
stacked.

# A non-constant coefficient of variation {#a-non-constant-coefficient-of-variation}

In step 4 we compared the fitted spread with the observed spread within each
concentration group. The 2050 colour fit had a local discrepancy at 0.96 µg/L.
Here we work through a third response whose coefficient of variation changes
systematically across concentrations, although the fitted family initially
assumes that it is constant. No convergence diagnostic detects this departure.

In each family with a free dispersion parameter (e.g., `Gamma`, `Beta` or
`negbinomial`), that parameter is constant along the series unless the formula
specifies otherwise. For a `Gamma` family under the identity link, a constant
`shape` is a constant coefficient of variation (i.e., the standard deviation of a
replicate is a fixed multiple of the fitted mean at each concentration). Where
replicate variation does not behave in this way, a single `shape` is estimated as
a compromise between the low-concentration and high-concentration ends of the
series, and does not describe either end.

## The assay

The `lum31` data contain the results of acute copper and zinc toxicity tests run
on the Lum-31 bioluminescent bacterial assay [@luter2025]. A suspension of marine
bacteria is dosed in a microplate well and its light output is read after a fixed
exposure, so the response is luminescence in relative light units.

Here we work through one plate of the copper series at 15 minutes (plate
`Cu 19Mar24 Rep1B`). A plate is a complete test (i.e., eleven concentrations by
four replicate wells). Because the plate reader sets its gain for each read,
plates are not on a common vertical scale, and taking a single plate avoids that
difference instead of modelling it. The group-level terms that handle the whole
assay, and the left-censoring that the blank correction requires, are described in
[*Grouping and factor
covariates*](https://open-aims.github.io/bayesnec/articles/example8.html).


``` r
data(lum31)
cu <- droplevels(subset(lum31, plate == "Cu 19Mar24 Rep1B" & minutes == 15))
c(wells = nrow(cu), concentrations = length(unique(cu$conc)),
  at_the_floor = sum(cu$censoring != "none"))
#>          wells concentrations   at_the_floor 
#>             44             11              1
```

This plate is one of two in the arm of
16 with the
fewest readings at the floor of the instrument (one of 44). A reading
held at a bound contributes a smaller spread than the well would have shown, so a
plate with many such readings would understate the very quantity examined in this
section.

Each concentration on one plate has four wells, so a coefficient of variation
computed within a concentration involves no curve, and cannot be inflated by any
lack of fit in the mean.


``` r
cv_obs <- tapply(cu$rlu_cens, cu$conc, function(z) sd(z) / mean(z))
round(cv_obs, 3)
#>     0.003 0.0137424  0.023888  0.044776  0.086552 0.1707008 0.3389984    0.6744    1.3458    2.6886 
#>     0.046     0.033     0.046     0.042     0.030     0.084     0.168     0.465     1.271     0.958 
#>    5.3742 
#>     0.876
```

The coefficient of variation is between 0.030 and
0.046 over the five lowest concentrations, then
rises without interruption to 1.271 at
1.3 mg/L, and eases
to 0.876 at the bottom of the series. The
largest of these values is 28 times the control
value, whereas a `Gamma` fitted with one `shape` returns a single value for all of
them.

## Fitting and screening the set

The copper response falls from its control, so `decline` is the candidate set. The
zinc series in this dataset rises above its control at low concentrations and also
needs the hormesis equations, which is why `all` is fitted to it in *Grouping and
factor covariates*.


``` r
gfam <- Gamma(link = "identity")
set_const <- bnec(rlu_cens | cens(censoring) ~ crf(log(conc), model = "decline"),
                  data = cu, family = gfam, seed = 17)
```


``` r
screened_const <- screen_models(set_const)
#> Dropping 1 of 11 candidate models that failed the sampler screen:
#>   -  ecxwb1p3: 39 divergent transitions
#> Fitted models are: nec3param nec4param ecxexp ecx4param ecxwb1 ecxwb2 ecxwb2p3 ecxll4 ecxll3 ecxflat
#> The fitted ecxflat curve does not fall to the control's 0.01 quantile within the predictor range for 7920 of 8000 draws. The NSEC summary is censored at 1.68: those draws keep their rank in it and are given no value.
best_const <- pull_best(screened_const)
#> Highest-weighted model is ecxwb1, holding 0.223 of the weight of 10 candidate models.
#> Pulling out model(s): ecxwb1
```


``` r
copper_axis <- list(
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log", breaks = c(0.003, 0.03, 0.3, 3),
                     labels = function(x) signif(x, 2)),
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) {
    format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
  }),
  labs(x = expression(paste("Copper (mg ", L^-1, ")")),
       y = "Relative light units")
)
autoplot(screened_const) + copper_axis
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-disp-autoplot-const-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-disp-autoplot-const" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-disp-autoplot-const</p>
</div>

The curve is the model-averaged prediction over the retained equations, shown with
its 95% credible band and with the model-averaged *N(S)EC* marked. The mean is
described well, with the response remaining above
91
per cent of its control value up to 0.045
mg/L, and falling to below one per cent by
0.34.

However, the band is the part of this figure to examine. It is a credible interval
on the *mean*, and at the control it is several hundred thousand relative light
units wide, whereas the four control wells span
117,000
between the lowest and the highest. An interval on a mean that is wider than the
observations from which the mean was estimated is what a dispersion parameter
fitted too large looks like once it is propagated to the curve. Below we test that
explanation, and examine what it does to the estimates.

15 equations were requested. `bnec_record()` shows that
3 were excluded before fitting and
1 failed to fit, which on 44
observations is the five-parameter equation, and the screen removed
1 more (all three mechanisms are covered
in steps 2 and 3).

## The probability integral transform

For a continuous response, the probability integral transform (PIT) value of an
observation is the proportion of the posterior predictive draws for that
observation that fall at or below it. A model that is right about the location and
the spread of each observation produces values spread uniformly over the unit
interval. A model that simulates more variability than the data contain produces
values crowded towards the middle, because an observation drawn from a narrower
distribution than the one simulated for it lands near the centre of those draws.
Conversely, a model that simulates less variability produces values crowded into
both ends.

`pp_check(type = "pit_ecdf")` plots the empirical distribution function of these
values against the uniform, between two dashed lines that a correctly specified
model stays inside with probability 0.99 over the whole interval at once.


``` r
pp_check(best_const, type = "pit_ecdf")
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-pit-const-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-pit-const" width="60%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-pit-const</p>
</div>


``` r
# pp_check() leaves the censored reading out, because the draws it compares it
# against are uncensored. The same subset is used here.
pit <- function(fit) {
  keep <- cu$censoring == "none"
  yrep <- posterior_predict(pull_brmsfit(fit))[, keep]
  colMeans(sweep(yrep, 2, cu$rlu_cens[keep], "<="))
}
pit_const <- pit(best_const)
round(c(middle_half = mean(pit_const > 0.25 & pit_const < 0.75),
        below_0.05 = mean(pit_const < 0.05),
        above_0.95 = mean(pit_const > 0.95)), 3)
#> middle_half  below_0.05  above_0.95 
#>       0.744       0.070       0.023
```

The curve runs along the lower dashed line from about 0.25 to 0.5, briefly falling
below it, and then rises steeply between about 0.55 and 0.65 towards the upper
line, without crossing it. This is the crowding towards the middle described
above, with 0.744 of the
values in the middle half of the interval, where 0.5 is expected, so the fit
simulates more variability than the observations contain. The band is wide because
it is drawn for 43 observations, and even so the
curve goes outside it.

## The concentrations the variance is wrong at

Because the transform pools all observations, it indicates that the calibration is
wrong, but not where along the series. That is answered by `check_fit()`, which
compares the observed spread within each concentration against the spread the fit
simulates there. On a single plate, each of its groups is the four wells at one
concentration, which is also the unit on which the coefficients of variation above
were computed.


``` r
cf_const <- check_fit(best_const)
cf_const[, c("group", "n", "obs_sd", "sim_sd", "sd_ratio", "ppp_sd", "control")]
#>        group n    obs_sd     sim_sd sd_ratio ppp_sd control
#> 1      0.003 4 48659.995 599854.829    0.081  0.999    TRUE
#> 2  0.0137424 4 34254.508 565623.746    0.061  1.000   FALSE
#> 3   0.023888 4 45273.800 542617.596    0.083  1.000   FALSE
#> 4   0.044776 4 40495.610 491427.679    0.082  0.998   FALSE
#> 5   0.086552 4 23064.931 314824.201    0.073  1.000   FALSE
#> 6  0.1707008 4 14403.575 107264.776    0.134  0.997   FALSE
#> 7  0.3389984 4  1143.009   3850.721    0.297  0.966   FALSE
#> 8     0.6744 4   221.393    205.997    1.075  0.460   FALSE
#> 9     1.3458 4   251.933    203.689    1.237  0.353   FALSE
#> 10    2.6886 4   513.008    202.938    2.528  0.040   FALSE
#> 11    5.3742 4   297.087    212.209    1.400  0.271   FALSE
```

`sd_ratio` is the observed spread divided by the simulated spread, so a value of 1
indicates agreement. Here it is between
0.06 and
0.08 over the five lowest
concentrations, then rises to a maximum of
2.53 at
2.7
mg/L, and 8 of the
11 groups are flagged. The fit simulates about
12 times the spread observed at
the control, and about 3 times too little where
the ratio is largest. A single `shape` cannot do both, which is what a constant
coefficient of variation requires of it.

## The dispersion sub-model

`disp("power")` writes `log(shape)` as a linear function of `log(mu)`, so that the
dispersion parameter becomes a function of the fitted mean instead of a constant.
The variance functions available, the families to which each applies, and what the
estimated exponent implies for a given family are described in [*Single model
usage*](https://open-aims.github.io/bayesnec/articles/example1.html).


``` r
set_power <- bnec(rlu_cens | cens(censoring) ~ crf(log(conc), model = "decline") +
                    disp("power"),
                  data = cu, family = gfam, seed = 17)
```


``` r
screened_power <- screen_models(set_power)
#> Dropping 1 of 11 candidate models that failed the sampler screen:
#>   -  ecxwb1: Rhat 1.013, ESS 108.8
#> Fitted models are: nec3param nec4param ecxexp ecx4param ecxwb2 ecxwb1p3 ecxwb2p3 ecxll4 ecxll3 ecxflat
#> The fitted ecxflat curve does not fall to the control's 0.01 quantile within the predictor range for 7920 of 8000 draws. The NSEC summary is censored at 1.68: those draws keep their rank in it and are given no value.
best_power <- pull_best(screened_power)
#> Highest-weighted model is ecxll4, holding 0.572 of the weight of 10 candidate models.
#> Pulling out model(s): ecxll4
```

The screen is run again, and not assumed. Here
1 equation fails it, and not the one that
failed before, because a dispersion sub-model changes the posterior from which
each equation is sampled. The highest-weighted equation also receives more of the
weight in this set than in the constant-dispersion set (the messages from
`pull_best()` name each), and the weights themselves are more concentrated: under
constant dispersion 5
equations share them, and under the sub-model
2 do.


``` r
brms::fixef(pull_brmsfit(best_power))[c("c0_Intercept", "c1_Intercept"), ]
#>               Estimate  Est.Error      Q2.5     Q97.5
#> c0_Intercept 4.5609622 0.25341306 4.0312072 5.0296814
#> c1_Intercept 0.7757112 0.07034322 0.6459906 0.9219484
```

`c1` is the exponent (a value of zero corresponds to the constant-dispersion
model), so an interval excluding zero supports non-constant dispersion. The
coefficients of variation computed above provide an estimate of this exponent that
involves no fit, because a power law makes `log(cv)` linear in `log(mu)`, with
slope `-c1/2`.


``` r
conc_mean <- tapply(cu$rlu_cens, cu$conc, mean)
obs_slope <- lm(log(cv_obs) ~ log(conc_mean))
# Multiplying by -2 reverses the order of the bounds, so the names confint()
# supplied would be attached to the wrong ends.
setNames(-2 * c(coef(obs_slope)[[2]], rev(confint(obs_slope)[2, ])),
         c("c1", "lower", "upper"))
#>        c1     lower     upper 
#> 0.7689298 0.6579071 0.8799526
c(r_squared = summary(obs_slope)$r.squared)
#> r_squared 
#> 0.9646321
```

The fitted and observed estimates agree. The fit gives
0.78
(0.65
to
0.92),
and the wells give 0.77
(0.66 to
0.88). This agreement indicates that
the sub-model describes the replicate variation the design measured, and does not
absorb a failure of the curve elsewhere in the series. A within-concentration
standard deviation involves no curve, which is what makes that comparison worth
making. Whether a power law is the right form for the relationship is a separate
question, which is answered here by the regression, with an R-squared of
0.965 on 9
degrees of freedom.


``` r
pp_check(best_power, type = "pit_ecdf")
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-pit-power-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-pit-power" width="60%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-pit-power</p>
</div>


``` r
pit_power <- pit(best_power)
round(c(middle_half = mean(pit_power > 0.25 & pit_power < 0.75),
        below_0.05 = mean(pit_power < 0.05),
        above_0.95 = mean(pit_power > 0.95)), 3)
#> middle_half  below_0.05  above_0.95 
#>       0.535       0.023       0.023
```

The curve stays between the dashed lines across the whole interval, and the middle
half contains 0.535 of
the values against the 0.5 expected, where the constant-dispersion fit placed
0.744. Because the
transform is computed from draws, on 43 observations
its tail counts are themselves noisy, and the middle half is the stable summary of
the three.

## The check repeated within concentrations

A transform computed over the whole fit is a weaker requirement than a comparison
made within each group, so we also repeat the group-wise check.


``` r
cf_power <- check_fit(best_power)
c(flagged = sum(cf_power$ppp_sd > 0.95 | cf_power$ppp_sd < 0.05),
  groups = nrow(cf_power),
  control_sd_ratio = round(cf_power$sd_ratio[cf_power$control], 3))
#>          flagged           groups control_sd_ratio 
#>            0.000           11.000            1.034
```

0 of the 11
groups are now flagged, against
8 before, and the control
is at 1.03 (as `sd_ratio`)
where it was 0.08. Both checks
therefore agree that the sub-model corrected what the checks found on the first
fit.

`plot()` draws each statistic against the spread that the fit simulates for it,
and takes both fits at once where a `model` column distinguishes the panels.
Because the response falls from about
1,060,000
relative light units at the control to about
198
at the bottom, we put the display on a logarithmic scale, as on a linear scale the
lower half of the series would be a row of points on the axis.


``` r
both <- rbind(cbind(cf_const, model = "constant"),
              cbind(cf_power, model = "disp(\"power\")"))
class(both) <- class(cf_const)
plot(both) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = function(x) {
    format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
  })
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-disp-checkfit-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-disp-checkfit" width="92%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-disp-checkfit</p>
</div>

Each bar is the 95% span of the statistic simulated from the fit, and each point
is the observed value. In the location panels the bars are wider under constant
dispersion, but all observed means fall inside their bars under both structures,
so the curve reproduces the response at all concentrations whichever dispersion
structure is used, and the mean was never what was wrong. The scale panels differ.
Under constant dispersion the observed standard deviation falls below its bar at
the 7 concentrations where the response is highest,
and the gap at the control is more than an order of magnitude
(48,700
observed, against a simulated span reaching
1,620,000).
Under the sub-model the bars close on the points, and all observed standard
deviations fall inside their bars, including that of the control
(48,700
against a span of
15,300
to
97,600).
A model can therefore describe the mean of each group and still be wrong about the
spread of all of them, which is the case singled out in the Overview, and here it
is the case that the sub-model corrects.


``` r
sd_ratios <- rbind(cbind(cf_const, dispersion = "constant"),
                   cbind(cf_power, dispersion = "disp(\"power\")"))
# check_fit() returns the group as a character label, so it is converted back
# before it can be drawn on a concentration axis.
sd_ratios$conc <- as.numeric(sd_ratios$group)
ggplot(sd_ratios, aes(x = conc, y = sd_ratio, colour = dispersion,
                      shape = dispersion)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log", breaks = c(0.003, 0.03, 0.3, 3)) +
  scale_y_continuous(transform = "log", breaks = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey35", "#1b6ca8")) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Copper (mg ", L^-1, ")")),
       y = "Observed / simulated residual SD", colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-sdratio-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-sdratio" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-sdratio</p>
</div>

The constant-dispersion series climbs across three orders of magnitude of the
predictor, passing through agreement near
0.67
mg/L. The `disp("power")` series stays near the dashed line, although its points
are not on it: its ratios run from 0.47 to
1.94, and on a logarithmic axis the low end
is as far from agreement as the high end. None of those groups is flagged, and
this appears to be a consequence of the design and not of the fit. A standard
deviation computed from four values has a sampling standard deviation of about
41 per cent of
itself, so four wells do not resolve a spread more finely than that. The display
therefore supports the conclusion that the ratios no longer trend with
concentration, but not that each one is exactly 1.

## The reported estimates

The estimates come from the screened set under the sub-model, shown here with its
credible band.


``` r
autoplot(screened_power) + copper_axis
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-autoplot-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-autoplot" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-autoplot</p>
</div>

The curve is the model-averaged prediction over the retained equations, and the
band is its 95% credible interval, both returned on the recorded concentration
scale, although the formula fitted `log(conc)`. The response remains above
91 per cent of its
control value up to 0.045 mg/L, is at
16 per cent of it by
0.17, and is below one per cent by
0.34, so the whole decline occurs
over a factor of about
8 in
concentration. The vertical lines mark the model-averaged *N(S)EC* and its bounds.

Compared with the constant-dispersion curve shown earlier (under *Fitting and
screening the set*), the band has closed onto the observations, and the *N(S)EC*
annotated on the figure has fallen with it. The curves under constant dispersion
and under the sub-model describe a common mean, and differ in how wide each makes
the posterior at the control, which is measured below.

The diagnostics above were run on the highest-weighted equation, which is the
model that `pp_check()` and `check_fit()` take. However, as in step 5, the
estimates are read from the screened set, because the weights here are spread
across several equations and no one of them describes the model-averaged value on
its own.


``` r
round(summary(screened_const)$mod_weights[, "wi"], 3)
#> nec3param nec4param    ecxexp ecx4param    ecxwb1    ecxwb2  ecxwb2p3    ecxll4    ecxll3   ecxflat 
#>     0.000     0.166     0.000     0.214     0.223     0.177     0.000     0.220     0.000     0.000
```


``` r
rbind(constant = nsec(screened_const, xform = exp),
      power = nsec(screened_power, xform = exp))
#>                 Q50       Q2.5      Q97.5
#> constant 0.10710285 0.04171873 0.14515901
#> power    0.05435925 0.03827005 0.06231398
rbind(constant = ecx(screened_const, ecx_val = 10, xform = exp),
      power = ecx(screened_power, ecx_val = 10, xform = exp))
#>                 Q50       Q2.5      Q97.5
#> constant 0.08742473 0.01716959 0.13691591
#> power    0.07225912 0.06765485 0.07856309
```

The *NSEC* falls from 0.107 to
0.054 mg/L, a factor of
2.0.
The change arises through the quantity from which `nsec()` reads its reference,
which is the posterior of the control mean with any group-level deviation
excluded.


``` r
control_reference <- function(fit) {
  nd <- data.frame(conc = min(cu$conc), censoring = "none")
  post <- posterior_epred(pull_brmsfit(fit), newdata = nd, re_formula = NA)[, 1]
  c(sd = sd(post), cv = sd(post) / mean(post),
    reference_share = unname(quantile(post, 0.01) / mean(post)))
}
round(rbind(constant = control_reference(best_const),
            power = control_reference(best_power)), 4)
#>                 sd     cv reference_share
#> constant 228509.53 0.1978          0.6510
#> power     13217.66 0.0131          0.9692
```

Under constant dispersion that posterior is
17
times wider. Because `nsec()` sets its reference at a lower quantile of it, the
reference is at
0.65 of the
control mean under constant dispersion, against
0.97 under the
sub-model. A reference placed that far below the control is crossed further along
the curve, so the constant-dispersion fit returns the *less* protective figure,
and nothing in its sampler diagnostics indicates this.

The EC10 changes by less, from
0.087 to
0.072 mg/L,
whereas its interval narrows from
0.120
to
0.011
mg/L. Because the EC10 is measured at a fixed fraction of the control mean, and
not at a quantile of its posterior, the variance assumption affects it through the
precision of the curve, and not through the placement of its reference. This is
the difference between the *NSEC* and the ECx described in the Overview.

A methods section should state the dispersion structure under which each estimate
was fitted, because constant dispersion and the sub-model return different
estimates from the same data.

# Summary

The sampler screen returned different outcomes for both prior choices on
the 2050 colour data. At the default sampling length, it removed
10 of 12 fitted equations
under uninformative priors and 7 of
11 under regularising priors. On `nassarius`, also at
the defaults, it removed 8 of
11. The equations and reasons should be
reported for each fit; a prior choice that reduces failures in one model may worsen
another.

The three outcomes have three different causes, and the purpose of the step is to
separate them. An equation that fails only on effective sample size has not been
given enough draws, and the remedy is to give it more. An equation that fails on
divergent transitions, or that fails to fit at all, indicates something about the
posterior. Where it is also the most heavily parameterised equation in the set,
and the design has few distinct concentrations, the explanation is that the
experiment does not contain the information the equation needs, and adjusting the
settings further to retain it is not the right response. The exclusion of an
equation that fails at the cutoff reflects a decision the analyst has taken, and
needs to be reported as one.

The variance assumption is the one that no sampler diagnostic detects. On the
`lum31` copper plate the observed coefficient of variation ran from
0.046 at the control to
0.876 at the bottom of the series, and the
constant-dispersion fit passed the sampler screen while simulating about
12 times the spread observed at
the control. Adding `disp("power")` brought all groups inside the flag, and halved
the model-averaged *NSEC*, from
0.107 to
0.054 mg/L. A fit can
therefore pass all the checks the sampler screen applies and still simulate the
wrong spread at the concentration from which both estimators are referenced.

This distinction also applies to the decisions made around the fit.
`binomial` was retained after the dispersion screen because the screen detected
nothing, not because nothing was there; the family for a continuous bounded
response was chosen on the support of the data and not on a test; and the scale on
which each estimate is reported depends on `xform`. None of these is a result that
the workflow produces automatically, and each is a decision that the analysis
needs to record.
